CausalChain: COL1A2 upregulation -> ECM remodeling -> Activation of integrin/FAK signaling -> (Phosphorylation/Transcriptional activation of NXF1 and THO complex) -> Specific export of pro-angiogenic/metastatic mRNAs -> Accelerated liver tumor progression
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, overexpression of COL1A2 leads to pronounced ECM remodeling, which in turn activates integrin-mediated FAK signaling. This activated signaling cascade elicits nuclear effects by phosphorylating key mRNA export machinery components (namely NXF1 and THO complex members) and by promoting the activity of transcriptional co-activators such as YAP/TAZ that upregulate these export factors. The combined effect enhances the selective export of mRNAs coding for proteins that drive angiogenesis and metastasis, thereby accelerating tumor progression. Targeted disruption of this COL1A2-integrin/FAK-nuclear export signaling axis using contemporary techniques like CRISPR interference, spatial transcriptomics, and phosphoproteomics will provide mechanistic insights and suggest therapeutic interventions to mitigate liver tumor aggressiveness.
Abstract: Liver tumor progression is conventionally linked to extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and integrin/FAK signaling; however, the mechanistic bridge between these extracellular events and nuclear mRNA processing remains poorly defined. Here, we propose that in liver cancers, COL1A2 overexpression induces aberrant ECM remodeling that potently activates integrin/FAK signaling. This cascade then mediates nuclear responses by (a) promoting selective phosphorylation of key nuclear mRNA export factors (e.g., NXF1 and components of the THO complex) and (b) inducing transcriptional regulators such as YAP/TAZ, which together enhance the expression and activity of the mRNA export machinery. This dual mechanism facilitates the preferential export of mRNAs encoding pro-angiogenic and metastatic proteins, thereby accelerating tumor progression. Utilizing state-of-the-art genomic and proteomic techniques—including CRISPR interference, spatial transcriptomics, and phosphoproteomics—this study aims to dissect and target the COL1A2-integrin/FAK to nuclear mRNA export axis to curb oncogenic mRNA export and reduce tumor aggressiveness.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that COL1A2-induced ECM remodeling activates integrin/FAK signaling, which then upregulates the nuclear mRNA export machinery (NXF1/THO complex) to enhance export of oncogenic mRNAs, promoting tumor progression. The revised hypothesis expands on this by addressing the mechanistic gap regarding how integrin/FAK signaling connects to nuclear export regulation. Specifically, the new model posits that FAK signaling acts both via post-translational modification (phosphorylation) of NXF1 and THO complex members and via the induction of transcriptional co-activators (e.g., YAP/TAZ) that boost expression of these components. Additionally, the revised hypothesis incorporates contemporary technological methods such as CRISPR interference, spatial transcriptomics, and phosphoproteomics to experimentally examine and modulate this signaling cascade, thereby enhancing its practical implementability.
